title: ABCDE assessment of the acutely unwell person
blurb: Assess and treat a deteriorating person systematically, fixing each life-threatening problem before moving on and calling for help early.
question: Mrs Sandhu, 72, is two days after bowel surgery. She is drowsy, breathing fast and her hands are cold. Using the ABCDE approach, what should the nurse assess and do first?

teach.h: One approach for every deteriorating person
teach.body: RCUK's ABCDE approach is the same for all deteriorating or critically ill patients: assess Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability and Exposure in that order. Treat each life-threatening problem before moving on, reassess regularly, check the effect of each treatment, call for help early and use the whole team so tasks happen at once. Communicate with SBAR. Plain English: fix what will kill first, then look again.

steps.label: Look and ask
steps.sub: 'How are you?' A normal reply: airway open, breathing, brain perfused

steps.label: Call for help
steps.sub: Ask a colleague to make sure help is coming

steps.label: Monitor early
steps.sub: SpO2, ECG, BP; IV access and bloods

teach.caption: Speaking in short sentences suggests a breathing problem. Failure to respond is a clear marker of critical illness.

letters.word: Disability: ACVPU or GCS, pupils, glucose

teach.h: Airway and Breathing: look for, then do
head: Look for
Do
rows: See-saw chest and abdomen, accessory muscles, noisy or absent breath sounds; cyanosis is late
Expert help now; airway opening, suction, adjuncts; high-concentration oxygen
RR (normal 12–20; above 25 is a warning), depth, equal expansion, SpO2, wheeze, stridor
Oxygen to target 94–98% (88–92% if hypercapnic risk); support ventilation if inadequate
teach.caption: Reservoir mask at 15 L/min for high-concentration oxygen. A pulse oximeter does not detect a rising carbon dioxide level.

teach.body: Look at the hands: colour and temperature. Measure capillary refill (normally under 2 seconds), pulse and BP. BP can stay normal in shock; a low diastolic suggests vasodilation, as in sepsis or anaphylaxis. Urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h is oliguria. Look for external or hidden bleeding, including when drains are empty. Treat: wide-bore cannula, bloods, and fluid as prescribed (RCUK general advice is 500 mL crystalloid over under 15 minutes if hypotensive, smaller volumes in heart failure; for sepsis follow NICE NG253).

Common causes of reduced consciousness are hypoxia, hypercapnia, poor brain perfusion and sedative or analgesic drugs, so review A, B and C first and check the drug chart (an antagonist such as naloxone may be needed for opioids). Check pupils, conscious level (ACVPU or GCS) and blood glucose. Nurse an unconscious person on their side if the airway is not protected. Then expose fully to examine, respecting dignity and minimising heat loss.

teach.h: Worked example: Mrs Sandhu on the surgical ward
items: A: she answers in short phrases, so her airway is open. The nurse pulls the emergency bell for help.
B: RR 30, SpO2 89% on air, no COPD. She starts oxygen to target 94–98% and listens: reduced sounds at the right base.
C: hands cold, CRT 4 seconds, pulse 118, BP 92/58. Abdominal drain empty but abdomen tense. She escalates to the doctor using SBAR: possible concealed bleeding or sepsis.
D: responds to voice (V on ACVPU), pupils equal, glucose 6.8 mmol/L. E: abdomen distended, wound oozing; she keeps her covered and warm.
She reassesses from A after each intervention and records all findings, treatments and responses.

teach.text: Do not finish the whole assessment before treating: fix A before B, B before C. And watch the fluid volume: the RCUK general bolus is 500 mL, but NICE NG253 uses 250 mL boluses for suspected sepsis in people aged 16 and over.

items: Same approach for every deteriorating person: A, B, C, D, E; treat as you go; reassess.
Call for help early and use the team; communicate with SBAR.
A: see-saw breathing and noisy or absent sounds mean obstruction, an emergency.
B: RR over 25 is a warning; oxygen to 94–98% (88–92% if hypercapnic risk).
C: CRT under 2 s is normal; oliguria is under 0.5 mL/kg/h; empty drains do not exclude bleeding.
D: think hypoxia, hypercapnia, perfusion, drugs; check pupils, ACVPU or GCS, glucose.

summary: You can now carry out an ABCDE assessment of an acutely unwell person, recognise the key signs at each step, and give the immediate treatment for each problem before moving on. You know to call for help early, reassess after every intervention and hand over with SBAR.

A.q: The nurse asks Mr Clarke, 70, 'How are you?' and he answers in full, normal sentences. According to RCUK, what does this tell her?
options: His saturation is above 94% on air
His blood pressure is within range
Airway open, breathing, brain perfused
No further assessment is needed now
A.why: RCUK: if the person responds normally, they have a patent airway, are breathing and have brain perfusion. The full ABCDE assessment still follows.

whyNot.0: Talking normally does not tell you the oxygen saturation; measure it.
whyNot.1: Speech does not confirm a normal blood pressure, which can be low in early shock.
whyNot.3: A normal reply is reassuring but does not replace a full ABCDE assessment.

A.q: During the airway assessment, which sign suggests airway obstruction?
options: A respiration rate of 22 per minute
See-saw movement of chest and abdomen
A capillary refill time of 3 seconds
A blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg
A.why: RCUK: airway obstruction causes paradoxical chest and abdominal movement ('see-saw' respirations) and use of accessory muscles.

whyNot.0: A rate of 22 is raised and scores on NEWS2, but it is a breathing finding, not a sign of obstruction.
whyNot.2: A prolonged capillary refill is a circulation finding.
whyNot.3: A low-normal blood pressure is assessed under circulation.

A.q: During the circulation assessment, below what hourly urine output is a catheterised adult described as oliguric?
options: 1.5 mL/kg/h
2 mL/kg/h
0.1 mL/kg/h
0.5 mL/kg/h
A.why: RCUK: oliguria is a urine volume under 0.5 mL/kg/h and is a sign of poor cardiac output.

whyNot.0: 1.5 mL/kg/h is above the oliguria threshold.
whyNot.1: 2 mL/kg/h is above the oliguria threshold.
whyNot.2: 0.1 mL/kg/h is far below the threshold; oliguria begins under 0.5.

B.q: Mr Hale, 64, has a high stoma output. He has cool peripheries, a pulse of 118 and BP 84/50. He has no heart failure. Which initial fluid bolus does RCUK's ABCDE guidance describe?
options: 500 mL crystalloid over under 15 minutes
250 mL crystalloid over 60 minutes
1,000 mL crystalloid over 4 hours
100 mL 20% glucose over 15 minutes
B.why: RCUK: give a bolus of 500 mL of crystalloid over less than 15 minutes if the patient is hypotensive, using smaller volumes (for example 250 mL) in known cardiac failure or trauma, and reassess.

whyNot.1: 250 mL is for known heart failure or trauma, and 60 minutes is too slow for a bolus.
whyNot.2: A litre over 4 hours is maintenance-speed, not resuscitation.

B.q: Mr Okafor, 58, is on morphine for post-operative pain. He is drowsy with a respiration rate of 7 and pinpoint pupils. The airway is supported. In assessing Disability, what should the nurse do?
options: Give a sugary drink to raise his glucose
Sit him up and recheck him in 1 hour
Review his drug chart and request naloxone
Give his next morphine dose for comfort
B.why: RCUK: check the drug chart for reversible drug-induced causes of reduced consciousness and give an antagonist where appropriate, such as naloxone for opioid toxicity.

whyNot.0: Nothing should be given by mouth to a drowsy person, and the picture suggests opioid toxicity.
whyNot.1: A respiration rate of 7 needs immediate action, not an hour's wait.
whyNot.3: More opioid would worsen his respiratory depression.

B.q: During the C assessment, Ms Ward's hands are cold, her capillary refill time is 4 seconds and her pulse is 118. What does this combination suggest?
options: Upper airway obstruction
Poor peripheral perfusion
Hypoglycaemia
Normal peripheral perfusion
B.why: RCUK: a capillary refill time over the normal (usually under 2 seconds) suggests poor peripheral perfusion; with cold hands and tachycardia this points to shock.

whyNot.0: Airway obstruction is identified in A by noisy or absent breathing and see-saw movement.
whyNot.2: Hypoglycaemia is checked in D with a glucose measurement, not by CRT.
whyNot.3: A CRT of 4 seconds is prolonged, not normal.

C.q: Mr Lee, 55, has no history of lung disease. On B assessment his respiration rate is 34 and SpO2 82% on air; he is struggling to speak. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Finish the whole ABCDE before treating
Give 2 L/min via nasal cannulae, move on
Check his blood glucose, then give oxygen
Reservoir mask at 15 L/min, then move on
C.why: RCUK: treat life-threatening problems before moving to the next step. Severe hypoxaemia needs high-concentration oxygen via a reservoir mask at 15 L/min (BTS: if SpO2 below 85%), aiming for 94–98%, while calling for help.

whyNot.0: Waiting until the end leaves life-threatening hypoxaemia untreated.
whyNot.1: 2 L/min is too little for severe hypoxaemia with an SpO2 of 82%.
whyNot.2: Glucose is checked in D; hypoxaemia in B must be treated first.

C.q: Mr Bello, 61, has central chest pain. His SpO2 is 97% on air. According to RCUK's immediate treatment for acute coronary syndrome, which statement about oxygen is correct?
options: Give 15 L/min, as for all chest pain
Give 4 L/min to protect the heart muscle
Aim for 100% saturation to rest the heart
It is not needed while SpO2 is 94% or more
C.why: RCUK: only give oxygen in suspected ACS if SpO2 is less than 94% breathing air. Record a 12-lead ECG early.

whyNot.0: High-flow oxygen for every chest pain is outdated and may cause harm.
whyNot.1: A routine low flow is not recommended when saturation is normal.
whyNot.2: Aiming for 100% is not recommended; avoid unnecessary oxygen.

C.q: During the E assessment of Mrs Sandhu, the nurse finds her abdominal drain bag empty, but her abdomen is tense and her BP is falling. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Escalate urgently as possible concealed bleeding
Reassure her, as the empty drain excludes bleeding
Flush the drain to check that it is patent
Record the drain output and review at 22:00
C.why: RCUK: intra-abdominal blood loss may be significant even if drains are empty. A tense abdomen with falling BP needs urgent escalation.

whyNot.1: An empty drain does not exclude internal bleeding.
whyNot.2: Flushing a surgical drain is not a nursing first response and delays escalation.
whyNot.3: Waiting until a later review leaves possible haemorrhage untreated.

reteach.title: A ladder you climb in order
reteach.question: Picture ABCDE as a ladder. Why can you not step onto C while B is broken?

blocks.h: Each rung holds up the next
blocks.body: No airway means no breathing; no oxygen means circulation and the brain fail. So you climb in order and repair each rung as you reach it: open the airway, give oxygen, support circulation, then look at the brain and the rest of the body. After any treatment, go back to the bottom rung and climb again.

blocks.text: A reassuring SpO2 on oxygen does not rule out a dangerously high carbon dioxide: the oximeter cannot detect hypercapnia.

explain.body: Complete an initial assessment and reassess regularly; treat life-threatening problems before moving on; assess the effect of treatment; call for help early; use the team; communicate with SBAR.

test.q: During an ABCDE assessment, when should a life-threatening problem be treated?
options: After all five steps are complete
Once the doctor has arrived
When it is found, before moving on
After observations are repeated
test.why: RCUK: treat life-threatening problems before moving to the next part of the assessment.

whyNot.0: Waiting until the end delays life-saving treatment.
whyNot.1: Nurses start immediate treatment while help is on its way.

explain.body: Obstruction: see-saw breathing, accessory muscles, noisy or absent sounds. Breathing: RR (12–20 normal), depth, expansion, SpO2, sounds. A pulse oximeter cannot detect hypercapnia.

test.q: A person with COPD has an SpO2 of 96% on 40% oxygen and is becoming drowsy. Why must the nurse not be reassured by the saturation?
options: Oximeters read low in COPD
SpO2 cannot show rising CO2
96% is below the COPD target
Drowsiness is unrelated to oxygen
test.why: RCUK: the pulse oximeter does not detect hypercapnia; on supplemental oxygen SpO2 may be normal with a very high carbon dioxide level.

whyNot.0: The issue is not a low reading but a normal reading hiding hypercapnia.
whyNot.2: 96% is above, not below, the usual 88–92% target in hypercapnic risk.
whyNot.3: Drowsiness may be caused by rising carbon dioxide from too much oxygen.

explain.body: Hands (colour, temperature), CRT, pulse, BP, urine output, bleeding. A low diastolic pressure suggests arterial vasodilation, as in sepsis or anaphylaxis.

test.q: According to RCUK, what does a low diastolic blood pressure suggest in an acutely unwell person?
options: Arterial vasodilation, as in sepsis
A blocked upper airway causing hypoxia
Severe hypoglycaemia needing glucose
A narrowed pulse pressure from bleeding
test.why: RCUK: a low diastolic blood pressure suggests arterial vasodilation, as in anaphylaxis or sepsis.

whyNot.1: Airway obstruction is assessed in A, not by blood pressure.
whyNot.2: Hypoglycaemia is identified by measuring glucose in D.
whyNot.3: A low diastolic with normal systolic widens, not narrows, the pulse pressure.

explain.body: Treat ABC causes first; review drugs; check pupils, ACVPU or GCS and glucose. Nurse an unconscious person on their side if the airway is not protected. Expose fully, keeping dignity and warmth.

test.q: An unconscious person is breathing but their airway is not protected. How should they be positioned?
options: Flat on their back
Sitting fully upright
In the lateral position
Prone with head turned
test.why: RCUK: nurse unconscious patients in the lateral position if their airway is not protected.

whyNot.0: Lying flat on the back risks the tongue and secretions blocking the airway.
whyNot.1: An unconscious person cannot maintain a sitting position or protect their airway upright.
whyNot.3: Prone positioning makes airway and breathing hard to monitor.
